lesson.title: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the IaaS, PaaS and serverless service models in AWS terms.
Describe Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations and Local Zones and why each exists.
Choose a Region using compliance, latency, service availability and price.
Apply the shared responsibility model to a developer's daily work.
Outline the four DVA-C02 exam domains this 30-day plan follows.
lesson.definition: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS runs this infrastructure in Regions around the world; each Region contains multiple isolated Availability Zones, and a global network of edge locations brings content closer to users.

theory.heading: Why developers use the cloud
theory.body: Instead of buying servers months in advance, a developer calls an API and receives a database, a queue or a function in seconds. This changes capital expense into variable expense, removes capacity guessing and lets teams experiment cheaply. For the Developer Associate exam the focus is on building with managed services, so you spend time on application logic rather than patching operating systems.
points: IaaS (EC2): you manage the OS, runtime and application.
PaaS (Elastic Beanstalk): AWS manages the platform; you deploy code.
Serverless (Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS): no servers to manage; you pay per request or per use.
Everything in AWS is an API call: the console, CLI, SDKs and CloudFormation all call the same APIs.

theory.heading: Regions and Availability Zones
theory.body: A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) or ap-south-2 (Hyderabad). Regions are isolated from each other so that a failure in one does not spread. Each Region has multiple Availability Zones (AZs), usually three or more; an AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to the other AZs by low-latency links. Deploying across at least two AZs is the basic pattern for high availability.
points: Most resources are Regional (Lambda, DynamoDB tables, SQS queues) or zonal (an EC2 instance, an EBS volume).
Some services are global: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront and AWS Organizations.
Data does not leave a Region unless you configure replication or transfer it.
AZ names such as ap-south-1a are mapped differently per account; AZ IDs (aps1-az1) are consistent.

theory.heading: Edge locations, Local Zones and Wavelength
theory.body: Edge locations (points of presence) are far more numerous than Regions and are used by CloudFront, Route 53, AWS Global Accelerator and Lambda@Edge to serve users with low latency. Local Zones place selected compute and storage close to large cities, and Wavelength Zones embed AWS inside telecom 5G networks. These exist because the speed of light is a hard limit: a user in Chennai served from us-east-1 sees roughly 200 ms round-trip time.
points: CloudFront caches responses at edge locations close to viewers.
Local Zones suit latency-sensitive workloads such as gaming or media rendering.
Edge locations do not host your general workloads; they cache and route.

theory.heading: Choosing a Region
theory.body: Region choice is a frequent interview question because it shows architectural judgement. The order matters: first legal and compliance requirements (data residency rules may require data to stay in India), then latency to users, then whether the services you need are available in that Region, and finally price, which differs between Regions.
points: Compliance and data residency: non-negotiable, filter first.
Proximity: lower latency to most users.
Service availability: new services and features often launch in a few Regions first.
Pricing: the same service can cost more in one Region than another.

theory.heading: Shared responsibility model
theory.body: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: physical data centres, hardware, the global network and the virtualisation layer. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud: IAM permissions, data encryption choices, network configuration and application code. The split moves with the service model: on EC2 you patch the guest OS; on Lambda AWS patches the runtime environment, but your code, dependencies and IAM role remain your job.
points: AWS: facilities, hardware, hypervisor, managed-service infrastructure.
Customer: data, IAM, encryption settings, security groups, application code.
The more managed the service, the less operational work for you.

theory.heading: The DVA-C02 exam at a glance
theory.body: The AWS Certified Developer – Associate exam tests whether you can build, deploy, secure and debug applications on AWS. It has four domains: Development with AWS Services (32%), Security (26%), Deployment (24%) and Troubleshooting and Optimization (18%). Questions are scenario-based, so this course explains why one service or setting fits a situation better than another.
points: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored) in 130 minutes; scaled score 100–1000, pass mark 720.
Multiple-choice and multiple-response questions with no penalty for guessing.

example.title: Inspecting Regions and AZs with the AWS CLI
example.body: Two read-only CLI calls show the infrastructure your account can use. The first lists enabled Regions; the second lists the AZs in Mumbai with their consistent zone IDs. Using --query (JMESPath) and --output table keeps the result readable.

code.source:
aws ec2 describe-regions --query "Regions[].RegionName" --output table

aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region ap-south-1 \
  --query "AvailabilityZones[].[ZoneName,ZoneId,State]" --output table

use_cases.title: Data residency for Indian fintech
use_cases.description: A payments start-up keeps customer data in ap-south-1 and ap-south-2 to meet regulatory requirements, using two Regions for disaster recovery inside India.

use_cases.title: Multi-AZ web application
use_cases.description: An application runs behind a load balancer across three AZs so that losing one data centre does not take the site down.

use_cases.title: Global content delivery
use_cases.description: An ed-tech platform serves video lessons through CloudFront edge locations so students across India get low-latency playback.

use_cases.title: Experiments without hardware
use_cases.description: A developer spins up a DynamoDB table and a Lambda function for a prototype, then deletes them the same day and pays only for usage.

demonstration.description: Use the AWS SDK for Python (boto3) to print how many AZs each of two Regions offers. The client is created per Region because most AWS APIs are Regional endpoints. Exact counts depend on your account and when you run it.

code.source:
import boto3

for region in ['ap-south-1', 'ap-south-2']:
    ec2 = boto3.client('ec2', region_name=region)
    zones = ec2.describe_availability_zones()['AvailabilityZones']
    names = [z['ZoneName'] for z in zones if z['State'] == 'available']
    print(region, len(names), names)

takeaways: A Region is an isolated geographic area; an AZ is one or more data centres inside it.
Use at least two AZs for high availability; use multiple Regions for disaster recovery or global users.
Choose a Region by compliance first, then latency, service availability and price.
IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are global; most other services are Regional.
AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure your data, permissions and code.
Every console click is an API call, which is why the CLI and SDKs can automate everything.

interview.question: What is the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone?
interview.answer: A Region is a geographic area containing multiple isolated Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more data centres with independent power and networking, connected to other AZs in the same Region by low-latency links.
interview.explanation: Strong answers add the purpose: AZs give fault isolation for high availability within a Region, while multiple Regions give disaster recovery and global reach.

interview.question: How would you choose a Region for a new application?
interview.answer: Filter by compliance and data residency first, then pick the Region with the lowest latency to most users, confirm every required service and feature is available there, and compare pricing.
interview.explanation: Interviewers listen for the order. Compliance is a hard constraint; latency, availability and cost are trade-offs.

interview.question: Explain the shared responsibility model with a Lambda example.
interview.answer: AWS manages the data centres, hardware, operating system and runtime patching for Lambda. The developer is responsible for the function code, its dependencies, the IAM execution role, environment-variable secrets and data encryption choices.
interview.explanation: Using a concrete managed service shows you understand that responsibility shifts with the service model rather than reciting a definition.

interview.question: Which AWS services are global rather than Regional?
interview.answer: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, AWS Organizations and WAF when attached to CloudFront are global. Services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS and S3 buckets are Regional, although S3 has a global namespace for bucket names.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the S3 nuance (global names, Regional buckets) is a common follow-up and shows precision.

interview.question: Your users are in India and Europe and the app must survive a full Region outage. What would you propose?
interview.answer: Deploy in two Regions (for example ap-south-1 and eu-west-1), each across multiple AZs, replicate data with DynamoDB global tables or S3 Cross-Region Replication, and route users with Route 53 latency-based routing plus health checks for failover.
interview.explanation: A strong answer separates AZ-level availability from Region-level disaster recovery and names concrete replication and routing services.

practice.title: Pick the best AWS Region
practice.objective: Apply the Region-selection order used by architects: compliance, required services, latency and then price.
practice.statement: Read the services your application needs, the countries where data is allowed to live, and a list of candidate Regions. A Region is eligible only if its country is allowed (or the allowed list is ANY) and it offers every required service. Among eligible Regions choose the lowest latency; break ties by the lower price index and then by Region name in alphabetical order. Print how many Regions are eligible and the selection.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: required services, comma-separated.
Line 2: allowed country codes, comma-separated, or ANY.
Line 3: n, the number of candidate Regions.
Next n lines: region country latency_ms price_index services (services comma-separated, no spaces).
practice.output_format:
Line 1: Eligible regions: <count>
Line 2: Selected: <region> (latency <ms> ms, price index <price>)
or NO SUITABLE REGION when none is eligible.

example.input:
lambda,dynamodb
IN
4
ap-south-1 IN 18 100 lambda,dynamodb,s3
ap-south-2 IN 25 95 lambda,dynamodb
ap-southeast-1 SG 60 105 lambda,dynamodb,s3
us-east-1 US 210 80 lambda,dynamodb,s3,bedrock
example.output:
Eligible regions: 2
Selected: ap-south-1 (latency 18 ms, price index 100)

constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 50; latency and price index are positive integers.
Country codes are compared in uppercase.
practice.starter:
required = [s.strip().lower() for s in input().split(',') if s.strip()]
allowed = input().strip().upper()
n = int(input())

# TODO: read the n candidates, filter them, then choose by latency, price, name
explanation: Store the required services as a set so a subset check (required <= offered) tests availability in one step.
Apply the hard constraints first: skip Regions in a disallowed country or missing a service.
Keep each eligible Region as a tuple (latency, price, name); Python compares tuples left to right, which is exactly the tie-break order.
min() of the tuples gives the answer; print NO SUITABLE REGION when the list is empty.

quiz.question: What best describes an AWS Availability Zone?
options: A geographic area that contains several Regions
A virtual network you create for your account
A single edge location used by CloudFront
One or more discrete data centres with independent power and networking inside a Region
quiz.explanation: An AZ is one or more isolated data centres within a Region. A VPC is the virtual network; edge locations serve CloudFront.

quiz.question: A healthcare company must keep patient records inside India, and most users are in Bengaluru. What should drive the Region decision first?
options: The Region with the lowest on-demand price
The Region with the most edge locations
The data residency requirement, which limits the choice to Indian Regions
The Region where new services launch first
quiz.explanation: Compliance is a hard constraint and is applied before latency, service availability or price.

quiz.question: Which of these services is global rather than Regional?
options: AWS Lambda
Amazon SQS
IAM
Amazon DynamoDB
quiz.explanation: IAM users, roles and policies are global to the account. DynamoDB tables, Lambda functions and SQS queues live in a specific Region.

quiz.question: Under the shared responsibility model, who patches the operating system that runs your AWS Lambda functions?
options: The developer, through a Lambda layer
The customer's operations team using Systems Manager
Nobody, because Lambda has no operating system
AWS, because Lambda is a managed service
quiz.explanation: For Lambda, AWS manages and patches the underlying OS and managed runtimes. You remain responsible for your code, dependencies and IAM role.

quiz.question: An application must keep running if a single data centre fails, at the lowest extra complexity. What is the standard design?
options: Deploy only to edge locations
Run copies in five Regions with manual failover
Run in a single AZ with larger instances
Deploy across at least two Availability Zones in one Region
quiz.explanation: Multi-AZ deployment within one Region handles the loss of a data centre. Multi-Region is for Region-level disaster recovery and adds more complexity.

lesson.title: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
objectives: Distinguish the root user, IAM users, groups and roles and when to use each.
Read and write an IAM policy document: Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource and Condition.
Compare identity-based, resource-based, AWS managed, customer managed and inline policies.
Explain why roles with temporary credentials are preferred over long-term access keys.
Match IAM actions and ARNs containing wildcards.
lesson.definition: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the global service that controls who can sign in (authentication) and what they can do (authorisation) in an AWS account. Identities such as users and roles receive permissions through JSON policy documents that allow or deny specific API actions on specific resources.

theory.heading: Identities: root, users, groups and roles
theory.body: The root user is created with the account and has unrestricted access; lock it with MFA and use it only for the few tasks that require it, such as changing the support plan. IAM users represent a person or workload with long-term credentials (a console password and/or access keys). Groups are collections of users used to attach permissions once; they cannot be nested and cannot be named as a principal in a policy. Roles have no long-term credentials: a trusted entity assumes the role and receives temporary credentials from STS.
points: Users: long-term credentials; today most organisations use IAM Identity Center for people instead.
Groups: only contain users, simplify permission management, cannot be nested.
Roles: assumed by AWS services (Lambda, EC2), other accounts, or federated users.
An EC2 instance gets a role through an instance profile; a Lambda function through its execution role.

theory.heading: Anatomy of a policy
theory.body: A policy is a JSON document with a Version (always "2012-10-17" for current features) and one or more Statements. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), the Action list (service:Operation, for example dynamodb:PutItem), the Resource ARNs the statement applies to, and an optional Condition block that narrows when it applies. Resource-based policies also include a Principal element naming who is granted access.
points: Actions and resources accept wildcards: * matches any sequence, ? matches one character.
Action names are case-insensitive; resource ARNs are case-sensitive.
NotAction and NotResource invert the match and are easy to misuse.
Conditions use keys such as aws:SourceIp, aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, aws:PrincipalTag/team or s3:prefix.

theory.heading: Types of policies
theory.body: Identity-based policies attach to a user, group or role and say what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach to a resource such as an S3 bucket, SQS queue, KMS key or Lambda function and say who can use it; they are essential for cross-account access. Managed policies are standalone and reusable: AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS, customer managed policies by you. Inline policies are embedded in one identity and deleted with it.
points: Prefer customer managed policies: versioned, reusable and auditable.
Use inline policies only for a strict one-to-one relationship.
Lambda resource-based policies grant services like S3 or API Gateway permission to invoke the function.
Permission boundaries and SCPs set maximum permissions; they never grant anything themselves (Day 3).

theory.heading: Least privilege and best practices
theory.body: Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources a workload needs. Broad policies such as AdministratorAccess on an application role turn a small bug or a leaked credential into a full account compromise. Start narrow, use IAM Access Analyzer to generate policies from CloudTrail activity and to find resources shared outside the account, and review last-accessed information to remove unused permissions.
points: Never create access keys for the root user; enable MFA on it.
Use roles for applications on AWS compute, never hard-coded keys.
Rotate any long-term access keys and remove unused ones.
Use tags and conditions (attribute-based access control) to scale permissions.

theory.heading: Roles in practice: trust policy plus permissions policy
theory.body: Every role has two policies that answer different questions. The trust policy (a resource-based policy on the role) answers who may assume the role, for example the service principal lambda.amazonaws.com. The permissions policy answers what the role may do once assumed. A common exam trap is an AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole: that is fixed in the trust policy, not the permissions policy.
points: Trust policy Principal examples: a service, an account ARN, a federated identity provider.
Permissions policy: identity-based policies attached to the role.

example.title: Least-privilege policy for an orders Lambda function
example.body: This customer managed policy lets a function read and write items in one DynamoDB table and write its own logs. It names exact actions and an exact table ARN instead of dynamodb:* on *, so a bug cannot delete other tables.

use_cases.title: Application roles
use_cases.description: Lambda functions, ECS tasks and EC2 instances receive roles so the SDK obtains rotating temporary credentials automatically.

use_cases.title: Team permissions through groups
use_cases.description: Developers, testers and auditors are placed in groups with different managed policies, so onboarding a person is one group membership.

use_cases.title: Cross-account access
use_cases.description: A CI/CD account assumes a deployment role in the production account; the role's trust policy names the CI/CD account.

use_cases.title: Service-to-service invocation
use_cases.description: A resource-based policy on a Lambda function allows an S3 bucket in the same account to invoke it on object upload.

demonstration.description: Create a role that Lambda can assume and attach the AWS managed basic execution policy using the CLI. The trust policy is passed as a file; the command output includes the role ARN you later give to the function.

code.source:
cat > trust.json <<'EOF'
{"Version": "2012-10-17",
 "Statement": [{"Effect": "Allow",
   "Principal": {"Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com"},
   "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"}]}
EOF

aws iam create-role --role-name orders-api-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json \
  --query Role.Arn --output text

aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name orders-api-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole

takeaways: Use roles and temporary credentials for workloads; avoid long-term access keys.
Groups hold users only, cannot be nested and cannot be a policy principal.
A policy statement is Effect + Action + Resource (+ Condition, + Principal for resource-based policies).
Trust policy = who can assume the role; permissions policy = what the role can do.
Resource-based policies enable cross-account and service-to-service access.
Least privilege limits the blast radius of bugs and leaked credentials.

interview.question: What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?
interview.answer: A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials such as a password or access keys. A role has no credentials of its own; a trusted principal assumes it and receives temporary credentials from STS that expire automatically.
interview.explanation: Add when to use each: roles for applications, AWS services and cross-account access; users only where long-term credentials are unavoidable.

interview.question: What are the main elements of an IAM policy statement?
interview.answer: Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (the API operations), Resource (the ARNs affected), an optional Condition block and, in resource-based policies, Principal.
interview.explanation: Mention Version 2012-10-17 and that action names are case-insensitive while ARNs are case-sensitive.

interview.question: Compare identity-based and resource-based policies.
interview.answer: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups or roles and define what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach to resources such as S3 buckets, SQS queues or KMS keys, include a Principal, and define who may access that resource, including principals from other accounts.
interview.explanation: The strong answer links resource-based policies to cross-account access and to services invoking Lambda.

interview.question: A Lambda function gets AccessDenied writing to DynamoDB. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.answer: Check the function's execution role: does its permissions policy allow the exact action (for example dynamodb:PutItem) on the exact table ARN, including the Region and account? Then look for explicit denies in boundaries or SCPs, KMS key permissions if the table uses a customer managed key, and read the error message, which names the action and resource.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want a methodical path: the role, action, ARN, then guardrails. Mentioning CloudTrail and the IAM policy simulator is a plus.

interview.question: When would you use an inline policy rather than a managed policy?
interview.answer: Only when the permissions must belong to exactly one identity and should be deleted with it. Managed policies are preferred because they are reusable, versioned and easier to audit.
interview.explanation: Showing that you know managed policies support version history and rollback adds depth.

practice.title: IAM wildcard permission checker
practice.objective: Practise how IAM matches actions and resource ARNs that contain * and ? wildcards.
practice.statement: A role has n Allow statements, each with one action pattern and one resource pattern. For each of m requests (an action and a resource ARN) print ALLOWED if at least one statement matches both, otherwise DENIED (IAM's implicit deny). In patterns, * matches any sequence of characters (including none and including / and :) and ? matches exactly one character. Actions match case-insensitively; resources are case-sensitive.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: n. Next n lines: action_pattern resource_pattern.
Next line: m. Next m lines: action resource.
practice.output_format: m lines: <action as given> -> ALLOWED or <action as given> -> DENIED

example.input:
2
s3:Get* arn:aws:s3:::reports/*
s3:ListBucket arn:aws:s3:::reports
3
s3:GetObject arn:aws:s3:::reports/2026/jan.csv
s3:PutObject arn:aws:s3:::reports/x.csv
S3:listbucket arn:aws:s3:::reports
example.output:
s3:GetObject -> ALLOWED
s3:PutObject -> DENIED
S3:listbucket -> ALLOWED

constraints: Patterns and values contain no spaces.
Only * and ? are special; every other character matches itself.
practice.starter:
import re
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().splitlines()
n = int(lines[0])

def compile_pattern(pattern, ignore_case):
    # TODO: turn * into .* and ? into . and escape everything else
    pass

# TODO: read statements and requests, print ALLOWED or DENIED
explanation: Convert each pattern to an anchored regular expression: * becomes .*, ? becomes . and every other character is escaped.
Compile action patterns with IGNORECASE because IAM action names are case-insensitive; resource patterns stay case-sensitive.
A request is allowed when any single statement matches both the action and the resource.
With no matching statement IAM falls back to the implicit deny, so print DENIED.

quiz.question: Which statement about IAM groups is true?
options: Groups can contain other groups
Groups can be named as the Principal in an S3 bucket policy
Groups contain users and are used to attach permissions to many users at once
Groups can be assumed like roles
quiz.explanation: Groups only contain users, cannot be nested, cannot be a policy principal and cannot be assumed.

quiz.question: An application on EC2 needs to read from S3. What is the most secure way to give it credentials?
options: Use the root user's access keys stored in environment variables
Embed the keys in the AMI
Attach an IAM role to the instance through an instance profile
Store an IAM user's access keys in the application's config file
quiz.explanation: An instance role delivers short-lived, automatically rotated credentials through the instance metadata service; no keys are stored.

quiz.question: A developer receives AccessDenied when calling sts:AssumeRole on a role in another account. Which policy most likely needs to change?
options: The S3 bucket policy in the target account
The role's permissions policy
The developer's group inline policy name
The role's trust policy, which must allow the caller as a principal
quiz.explanation: The trust policy controls who may assume a role. The caller also needs sts:AssumeRole allowed in their own identity policy.

quiz.question: Which IAM policy element appears in resource-based policies but not in identity-based policies?
options: Action
Condition
Effect
Principal
quiz.explanation: Resource-based policies must say who is granted access, so they include Principal. Identity-based policies apply to the identity they are attached to.

quiz.question: A statement allows the action s3:Get* on arn:aws:s3:::logs/*. Which request does it allow?
options: s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::logs/app.log
s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::logs
s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::logs/2026/app.log
s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::LOGS/app.log
quiz.explanation: s3:Get* matches GetObject, and the resource wildcard * matches 2026/app.log including the slash. ARNs are case-sensitive, so LOGS does not match.

questions.topic: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
questions.question: Explain the shared responsibility model with a Lambda example.
questions.answer: AWS manages the data centres, hardware, operating system and runtime patching for Lambda. The developer is responsible for the function code, its dependencies, the IAM execution role, environment-variable secrets and data encryption choices.
questions.explanation: Using a concrete managed service shows you understand that responsibility shifts with the service model rather than reciting a definition.

questions.topic: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
questions.question: Which AWS services are global rather than Regional?
questions.answer: IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, AWS Organizations and WAF when attached to CloudFront are global. Services such as Lambda, DynamoDB, SQS and S3 buckets are Regional, although S3 has a global namespace for bucket names.
questions.explanation: Mentioning the S3 nuance (global names, Regional buckets) is a common follow-up and shows precision.

questions.topic: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
questions.question: Your users are in India and Europe and the app must survive a full Region outage. What would you propose?
questions.answer: Deploy in two Regions (for example ap-south-1 and eu-west-1), each across multiple AZs, replicate data with DynamoDB global tables or S3 Cross-Region Replication, and route users with Route 53 latency-based routing plus health checks for failover.
questions.explanation: A strong answer separates AZ-level availability from Region-level disaster recovery and names concrete replication and routing services.

questions.topic: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
questions.question: What is the difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?
questions.answer: A user is a long-lived identity with permanent credentials such as a password or access keys. A role has no credentials of its own; a trusted principal assumes it and receives temporary credentials from STS that expire automatically.
questions.explanation: Add when to use each: roles for applications, AWS services and cross-account access; users only where long-term credentials are unavoidable.

questions.topic: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
questions.question: What are the main elements of an IAM policy statement?
questions.answer: Effect (Allow or Deny), Action (the API operations), Resource (the ARNs affected), an optional Condition block and, in resource-based policies, Principal.
questions.explanation: Mention Version 2012-10-17 and that action names are case-insensitive while ARNs are case-sensitive.

questions.topic: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
questions.question: Compare identity-based and resource-based policies.
questions.answer: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups or roles and define what that identity can do. Resource-based policies attach to resources such as S3 buckets, SQS queues or KMS keys, include a Principal, and define who may access that resource, including principals from other accounts.
questions.explanation: The strong answer links resource-based policies to cross-account access and to services invoking Lambda.

questions.topic: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
questions.question: A Lambda function gets AccessDenied writing to DynamoDB. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: Check the function's execution role: does its permissions policy allow the exact action (for example dynamodb:PutItem) on the exact table ARN, including the Region and account? Then look for explicit denies in boundaries or SCPs, KMS key permissions if the table uses a customer managed key, and read the error message, which names the action and resource.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want a methodical path: the role, action, ARN, then guardrails. Mentioning CloudTrail and the IAM policy simulator is a plus.

questions.topic: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
questions.question: When would you use an inline policy rather than a managed policy?
questions.answer: Only when the permissions must belong to exactly one identity and should be deleted with it. Managed policies are preferred because they are reusable, versioned and easier to audit.
questions.explanation: Showing that you know managed policies support version history and rollback adds depth.

days.title: AWS Cloud Fundamentals and Global Infrastructure
days.focus: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. AWS runs this infrastructure in Regions around the world; each Region contains multiple isolated Availability Zones, and a global network of edge locations brings content closer to users.
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the IaaS, PaaS and serverless service models in AWS terms.
Describe Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations and Local Zones and why each exists.
Choose a Region using compliance, latency, service availability and price.
Apply the shared responsibility model to a developer's daily work.
Outline the four DVA-C02 exam domains this 30-day plan follows.
days.assignment: Read the services your application needs, the countries where data is allowed to live, and a list of candidate Regions. A Region is eligible only if its country is allowed (or the allowed list is ANY) and it offers every required service. Among eligible Regions choose the lowest latency; break ties by the lower price index and then by Region name in alphabetical order. Print how many Regions are eligible and the selection.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: A Region is an isolated geographic area; an AZ is one or more data centres inside it.
Use at least two AZs for high availability; use multiple Regions for disaster recovery or global users.
Choose a Region by compliance first, then latency, service availability and price.
IAM, Route 53 and CloudFront are global; most other services are Regional.
AWS secures the cloud itself; you secure your data, permissions and code.
Every console click is an API call, which is why the CLI and SDKs can automate everything.

days.title: IAM Users, Groups, Roles and Policies
days.focus: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the global service that controls who can sign in (authentication) and what they can do (authorisation) in an AWS account. Identities such as users and roles receive permissions through JSON policy documents that allow or deny specific API actions on specific resources.
objectives: Distinguish the root user, IAM users, groups and roles and when to use each.
Read and write an IAM policy document: Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource and Condition.
Compare identity-based, resource-based, AWS managed, customer managed and inline policies.
Explain why roles with temporary credentials are preferred over long-term access keys.
Match IAM actions and ARNs containing wildcards.
days.assignment: A role has n Allow statements, each with one action pattern and one resource pattern. For each of m requests (an action and a resource ARN) print ALLOWED if at least one statement matches both, otherwise DENIED (IAM's implicit deny). In patterns, * matches any sequence of characters (including none and including / and :) and ? matches exactly one character. Actions match case-insensitively; resources are case-sensitive.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Use roles and temporary credentials for workloads; avoid long-term access keys.
Groups hold users only, cannot be nested and cannot be a policy principal.
A policy statement is Effect + Action + Resource (+ Condition, + Principal for resource-based policies).
Trust policy = who can assume the role; permissions policy = what the role can do.
Resource-based policies enable cross-account and service-to-service access.
Least privilege limits the blast radius of bugs and leaked credentials.
